newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel must focus on budget cuts and peace - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Israel must focus on budget cuts and peace - IMF.

text.p: In a report on Israel, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Monday highlighted the importance of containing government spending and keeping the Middle East peace process on track.
"Adverse security developments would undo the improvement in domestic and external confidence that has occurred over the past several years," it said in its 1996 staff appraisal report on Israel.

"The imbalance in (the fiscal) accounts is at the core of the current strains (in the economy) and it is essential that the deficit target for 1997 be achieved, over-achieved if growth rates proves stronger than expected," the IMF said.
The Treasury is trying to keep Israel's 1997 budget deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product and is seeking 6.1 billion shekels ($1.86 billion) in spending cuts.
The report noted that in its "restive mixture of promise and risk" Israel's economy had considerable growth potential.

"The dynamism of the business sector is particularly notable, the capital stock is up to date and exports are well-diversified and increasingly focused on internationally competitive, high value-added products," the IMF said.
The IMF said, however, that to fulfil its "striking" promise for future growth, Israel would have to take measures to reduce public sector wages, subsidies, transfer payments and tax preferences.
It said the government must be prepared for further revenue shortfalls in 1997 by making significant budgetary reserves.
Over the long term, the IMF expressed doubt that the Treasury's long-term goal of reducing the budget deficit to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product in the year 2001 was sufficient.
"More ambitious deficit targets are needed," the IMF said. "The existing ones should at least be viewed as minimum objectives".

The IMF supported the Bank of Israel's strict monetary policy of the last two years. It said that once the Israeli government's budget deficit had been contained, the central bank could ease its stance, but only to a limited degree.

"Care must be taken to ensure that disinflation also remains firmly on the intended track," the report said. "This will require that interest rates remain significantly positive in real terms over the medium term, as well as steadfast pursuit of fiscal consolidation."
The report also urged Israel to step up the pace of market-oriented structural reform, particuarly through privatisation.
The IMF indicated it supported the capital market reforms proposed by the Brodet committee last October, which aim to encourage long-term savings.
However, the IMF said the Brodet recommendations are not enough.
